newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Minister denounces "sabotage" of Madagascar polls.
newsitem.headline: Minister denounces "sabotage" of Madagascar polls.

text.p: The people of Madagascar went to polling stations on Sunday to elect a new president, and the interior minister denounced what he said were attempts to sabotage the election in the Indian Ocean island.
Many polling stations in the capital Antananarivo were crowded when they opened at 6 a.m. local (0300 GMT), but voting moved more slowly later.
The election had to be called after President Albert Zafy, who took office in 1993 from a former military ruler, was impeached by parliament in July for abuse of his authority.
With at least five strong candidates in a field of 15, political analysts doubted an outright winner would emerge from Sunday's vote. No date has been set for the expected run-off.

Several hours after voting started, Interior Minister Charles Sylvain Rabotoarison denounced what he said were attempts to sabotage the election, saying police in the capital had received reports of various irregularities.
Speaking on Radio Madagascar, he cited instances of "phantom electoral lists", voters' cards for under-age people and people with three or four voters' cards. The reports were being investigated.
By midday, the radio estimated that only 10-25 percent of those eligible had voted at the 15,000 polling stations, raising speculation that the final turnout would be low.
Voting would last 12 hours. First results were expected on Sunday night and final results several days later.
Many intending voters complained that their names did not appear on the poll register, and some voters said they had been offered bribes to support a particular candidate.
Joint patrols of police and soldiers took to the streets when the polls opened, but maintained a low-key presence.
Preachers and pharmacists, admirals and Marxists, aristocrats and traders were among the 15 candidates vying to take charge of the vast island and its 14 million people who live in chronic poverty.
Former president Zafy, 69 and known for his trademark straw hat, was a leading contender despite the constitutional court's endorsement in September of his impeachment.
So were the former military ruler he defeated in 1993, Didier Ratsiraka, and the current prime minister and interim president, Norbert Ratsirahonana.
U.S.-educated millionaire Herizo Razafimahaleo and Richard Andriamanjato, a Marxist pastor who is speaker of the national assembly, were also expected to score well.
Razafimahaleo, the youngest of the front-runners at 41, hired a helicopter to dash around the island pulling in crowds of mainly young people, while rivals bounced along pot-holed roads by car.
The high level of support during campaigning for retired admiral Ratsiraka, 59, surprised analysts. He returned from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September.
He was reviled by many of his people in the early 1990s for using the army to resist the pro-democracy movement.
